strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear identification of HLS development bottlenecks and practical relevance
VODA (Verification-Oriented Data Augmentation) is a pragmatic paradigm for dynamically capturing and expanding error case datasets
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with 612 test cases across 33 HLS designs and 34 error types, including comparisons with multiple LLM baselines and existing methods
Thorough ablation studies demonstrating the contribution of individual components (fine-tuning, analysis agent, DPO, iterative refinement)
Strong empirical results: 82.7% pass rate on error repair (17% improvement over GPT-4o), 3.6× geometric mean speedup on optimization tasks
Clear system architecture and well-designed multi-agent framework with specialized agents for distinct phases (generation, debugging, optimization)
Effective presentation with informative figures and workflow diagrams
weaknesses: CRITICAL: Fundamental scope mismatch with ACL—this is a hardware design automation paper, not a computational linguistics or NLP contribution. The work does not address core language understanding, linguistic modeling, or NLP methodologies, and would be far more appropriate for DAC, ICCAD, or hardware design conferences

Limited novelty in LLM/NLP methodology: uses standard LoRA fine-tuning, applies existing DPO technique without domain adaptation, and employs straightforward error-type-based agent routing with no linguistic or LLM architectural innovation

Data construction quality concerns: Insufficient validation that LLM-injected bugs are realistic; unclear breakdown of how many error types were discovered vs. manually enumerated; no demonstration that synthetic bugs trigger similar failure modes as real errors

Limited experimental scope: Only 5 linear algebra kernels (PolyBench) used for optimization evaluation, providing minimal algorithmic diversity; evaluation tied to proprietary Xilinx ZCU106 hardware with no evidence of generalization to other platforms or HLS tools

Reproducibility issues: Relies on proprietary Xilinx Vitis HLS tool (expensive, non-open-source); no mention of code/dataset release; missing critical implementation details (exact prompts, HLS output parsing, RAG mechanism, latency measurements)

Evaluation methodology limitations: Unfair comparison with general LLMs (expected that fine-tuned models outperform)—lacks nuance; incomplete baselines (HeteroRefactor, HeteroGen mentioned but not compared); ad-hoc energy efficiency proxy metric (Eq. 2) with unjustified functional forms; no user studies or practical utility validation

Insufficient failure analysis: 17.3% failure rate not analyzed; no breakdown of error types that remain unsolved or design patterns that break the system; limited discussion of out-of-distribution behavior

Generalization claims inadequately supported: Only 5 test kernels limit statistical significance of generalization claims; no analysis of how performance scales to diverse problem types or larger designs

Training details underspecified: No ablation on hyperparameter choices (why 11 epochs SFT + 3 epochs RL?); preference dataset construction for DPO (3,489 pairs) not well documented; no multi-run statistics or confidence intervals reported

System cost analysis missing: No latency measurements for full optimization+debugging cycle; up to 5 iterations required in some cases with no analysis of iteration distribution; no practical computational budget validation

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing real HLS design bottlenecks (data scarcity, design space exploration, debugging complexity)
Comprehensive system design with principled multi-component architecture and clear separation of concerns
Strong empirical results: 93.4% debugging pass@1 vs 60.6% for Gemini-3-pro; 18.1× speedup over baseline; post-implementation validation confirms feasibility
Thoughtful dataset construction including VODA's self-evolving error mechanism and 33-category BugRAG, with proper train-test separation analysis
Thorough experimental validation with ablation studies, multiple benchmarks (108 generation tasks, 591 debugging cases), and comprehensive baseline comparisons
Detailed reproducibility documentation covering training settings, prompt design, and experimental protocols
weaknesses: Critical scope mismatch: This is hardware design automation research, not computational linguistics. It lacks novel NLP/CL methodology and would be better suited for DAC, ICCAD, or ASPLOS venues rather than ACL

Significant practical limitations severely restrict applicability: only supports loop-level directives (PIPELINE, UNROLL, ARRAY_PARTITION), excludes critical DATAFLOW and AXI interfaces, validated on single hardware platform (Xilinx ZCU106)
Heavy dependence on specialized fine-tuning of Qwen-2.5-Coder-14B; unclear how much improvement derives from system design vs. fine-tuning; generalization to other LLM families unexplored
Circular reasoning in VODA: using LLM-generated errors to train LLMs to fix LLM-generated errors; unclear transfer to human-written buggy code; no evaluation on real human bugs

Insufficient experimental rigor: no statistical significance testing or error bars on pass rates; limited baseline scope; unfair comparisons to general-purpose LLMs not designed for HLS; small optimization dataset (4,804 samples from 20 kernels) raises overfitting concerns
Reproducibility limitations: fine-tuned models and code not provided; dependency on proprietary Xilinx Vitis HLS 2022.1; no public dataset release mentioned
Unclear generalization: no evaluation on HLS patterns outside training distribution, mixed loop+dataflow designs, or larger complex designs; no failure mode analysis

CoT generation bias and circular logic: teacher model introduces implicit biases; RAG baseline in Section E.1 may reflect suboptimal chunking rather than RAG limitations; alternative CoT strategies not explored
